resources.string: Histamine-containing granules
Mast cells store histamine and other mediators in granules for release during an immune response.
Tissue-resident cell
This cell sits in tissue outside the vessel. It is not a circulating basophil.
Hematopoietic stem cell
A marrow stem cell can self-renew and give rise to blood lineages. Shape alone does not establish identity.
Marrow niche
Nearby cells and the vascular environment help maintain the stem-cell niche.
Cell contact
The illustration represents a helper T cell communicating with an antigen-presenting cell.
Coordination signals
Signals from helper T cells can support other immune cells. The colors illustrate roles, not staining.
Target contact
The illustration shows contact with a recognized target cell, not indiscriminate damage.
Granules near the contact
An activated cytotoxic T cell can induce a closely contacted target cell to undergo programmed cell death.
Regulatory interaction
Regulatory T cells help restrain some immune responses. This panel shows a functional example, not a pathologic sample.
Neighboring immune cell
The right-hand cell is only a neighboring cell. It is not a second regulatory T cell.
Pericyte on the outside
A pericyte lies on the outer surface of the microvessel, not in the bloodstream.
Supporting process
Processes extend around the vessel and contribute to microvascular support and signaling.
Overlapping endothelial edges
This initial lymphatic capillary example shows overlapping edges that can admit interstitial fluid.
Lymphatic lumen
The lumen is the collecting space. This is not a valve of a larger collecting vessel.
Supported germ cells
Sertoli cytoplasm spans much of the seminiferous epithelium and contacts developing germ cells.
Sertoli-cell junction
Junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells help form the blood–testis barrier.
Basal compartment
Spermatogonia are near the basal lamina. Some self-renew and others enter differentiation.
Basal lamina
This line is the boundary of the seminiferous epithelium.
Primary spermatocyte
This more luminal example illustrates a cell in meiosis I, distinct from the basal spermatogonium.
Paired homologs
The marks illustrate chromosome pairing, not the actual number or appearance of all chromosomes.
Motile cilia
Cilia on the uterine-tube epithelium support luminal transport alongside smooth muscle motion.
Epithelial fold
The highlighted cell sits on a mucosal fold facing the uterine-tube lumen.
Lumen-facing surface
This example is in the epithelial lining. It differs from the underlying endometrial stroma.
Gland epithelium
Some epithelial cells line uterine glands and produce secretions.
Stromal cell
Stromal cells lie below the lining and contribute to the supportive endometrial tissue.
Extracellular matrix
The surrounding matrix helps organize the tissue. This is not a personal cycle-stage prediction.
Milk-facing surface
Luminal cells line secretory units and release milk components into the lumen.
Adjacent myoepithelium
The outer contractile layer helps eject existing milk; it is not the milk-producing lining.
Outer trophoblast layer
This villus example shows the multinucleated outer layer contacting maternal blood.
Villus core
The internal villus contains fetal vessels. The drawing does not merge maternal and fetal blood.
Epidermal dendrite
Processes extend among keratinocytes and can sample the epidermal environment.
Langerhans cell body
This is an epidermal immune cell, distinct from a sensory nerve ending.
Lipid droplets
Maturing sebocytes accumulate lipids that contribute to sebum.
Outlet toward the follicle
The gland empties into the follicle in this example. It is not the eccrine sweat duct.
Secretory surface
Cells in the eccrine coil form the initial fluid in the lumen. The duct subsequently modifies it.
Coil lumen
This is a section through the secretory coil, not the skin pore.
Matrix in the hair bulb
Dividing matrix cells contribute descendants to the growing hair and its inner sheath.
Adjacent dermal papilla
The papilla belongs to the supportive dermal tissue, not the matrix cell layer.
Muscle satellite cell
The highlighted cell lies between the basal lamina and the muscle fiber membrane.
Existing muscle fiber
The fiber is separate from the satellite cell. Satellite descendants can support repair, but this is not a recovery forecast.
Elongated nucleus
In this lengthwise view, a slender tendon cell lies between collagen bundles.
Collagen bundles
These extracellular fibers run mainly along the tendon. A short cell extension contacts the surrounding matrix.
Sweat duct
Sweat travels up this duct. Cells lining the duct can reabsorb some salts.
Skin pore
The duct opens at the skin surface. Liquid that evaporates there can remove heat.
Hair shaft
The shaft above the surface consists mainly of keratinized cells. Their living precursors are in the bulb.
Dermal papilla
The papilla lies inside the base of the bulb and contains connective tissue and capillaries.

This models heat required for evaporation near 30°C. It does not calculate whole-body heat balance, skin temperature, sweat rate, or dehydration.
Eccrine example. Liquid secretion, duct transport and evaporation are different events. Animation speed does not represent their real timing.
A schematic of a follicle cycle. Stage lengths vary, and this view does not determine whether an individual follicle is growing.
Sweat secretion and evaporation
The eccrine coil produces initial sweat
Sweat moves through the duct as its composition changes
Sweat reaches a pore on the skin surface
The part that evaporates absorbs heat
Hair follicle cycle
Matrix cells divide during active growth
Their descendants contribute to the keratinized shaft
The lower follicle regresses during transition
The follicle rests before restarting growth
